BFGS method

Synopsis


  use oakleaf

  type, abstract, public :: bfgs_function
   contains
     procedure(fvalue), deferred :: val
     procedure(fgradient), deferred :: grad
     procedure :: fungrad => fungradient
     procedure :: hess => fhessian
     procedure :: maxalf => maxalpha
     procedure :: break => breaker
  end type bfgs_function

  abstract interface

     real(REAL64) function fvalue(this,x)
       import :: REAL64, bfgs_function
       class(bfgs_function), intent(in) :: this
       real(REAL64), dimension(:), intent(in) :: x
     end function fvalue

     subroutine fgradient(this,x,fgrad)
       import :: REAL64, bfgs_function
       class(bfgs_function), intent(in) :: this
       real(REAL64), dimension(:), intent(in) :: x
       real(REAL64), dimension(:), intent(out) :: fgrad
     end subroutine fgradient

  end interface

  subroutine bfgsmin(fcn,x,H,gtol,maxiter,verbose,report_file,iflag)

    class(bfgs_function), intent(in) :: fcn
    real(REAL64), dimension(:), intent(in out) :: x
    real(REAL64), dimension(:,:), intent(out) :: H
    real(REAL64), intent(in) :: gtol
    integer, intent(in) :: maxiter
    logical, intent(in) :: verbose
    character(len=*), intent(in) :: report_file
    integer, intent(out) :: iflag

  end subroutine bfgsmin

Description

The bfgsmin is a general optimisation routine based on the BFGS method. The procedure search for a minimum of a non-linear function f(x), x ∈ Rn by the Newton-Raphson method with help of the gradient 𝛻 f(x) and the quasi-Newton estimation of the Hessian. The function should be strictly convex without any constrains and fully determined (i.e. all variables are independent). It is considered as a counterpart of the Marquard-Levenberg method, especially the routines lmder(),lmdif() of Minpack; the minimised function is be general rather than a sum of squares.

The line search, based on the backward-search, is used. It can handle constraints if the minimum is inside of the feasible region (nor on the border). As the linear search parameter can be controlled, the principal drawback of the parameter search in Marquard-Levenberg method is removed. It is useful for the scale estimation of Huber's regression and similar cases.

The success of the finding of the global minima depends on initial estimates for non-linear functions having multiple local ones. A suitable initial estimate leads to fast convergence.

The algorithm is simple, stable and reliable, but the convergence is slow and the function approximation can be poor compared to trust-region methods.

Parameters

fcn
[in] is an abstract function carrying the minimisation function itself and the gradient, see below.
x
[in out] The array of initial estimates on the input, and the reached solution on the output.
H
[out] an approximation the inverse quasi-Hessian in the minimum. The covariance matrix, as well as statistical errors of parameters, are computed based on.
gtol
[in] the tolerance for the convergence finish as the Euclidean norm of the gradient. The square root of machine epsilon (10-8) is safe choice, if elements of the gradient are small, value about 10-13 is enough.
maxiter
[in] The maximal amount of iterations. Recommended value is about two hundredth per variable. Usually a few thousands is enought.
verbose
[in] Be, or not to be, verbose.
report_file
[in] A file to store intermediate steps, if a non-empty string is passed. Consult the program listing for details.
iflag
[out] A result flag; the values 0,1 indicates success, value 6 is a fail. If |𝛻 f(x)| < gtol, iflag is 0, if moreover |fi+1(x) - fi(x)| < ϵ (machine epsilon), iflag is 1. If interrupted by user, iflag = 9.

The implementation is in src/bfgs.f08.

The function

The minimised function is defined as a derived type object. The user must specify its functional value f(x) and the gradient 𝛻 f(x). If data are required, they are stored in the derived type, see the example below.

fcn % val()
(mandatory) The function calculate the functional value f(x).
fcn % grad()
(mandatory) The subroutine evaluate of the gradient 𝛻 f(x).
fcn % fungrad()
The subroutine compute both the value and the gradient together; it can improve the speed.
fcn % hess()
The analytic Hessian, in fact, it is not used in any calculations. By default it is computed numerically.
fcn % maxalpha()
The scalar search parameter, purpose of this routine is to keep the solution inside the feasible region.
fcn % break()
The purpose of this function is to offer a possibility to interrupt the optimisation process by user. It is called once per iteration.

Example

We wish to estimate of parameters a,b of the line y ≈ ax + b by method of least squares. The function implementation should have been in the module, to generate the external interface. Save the program to the file line.f08: 

module lajna

  use bfgs_method
  use iso_fortran_env
  implicit none

  type, extends(bfgs_function) :: line_function
     real(REAL64), dimension(:), pointer :: x,y
   contains
     procedure :: val => lvalue
     procedure :: grad => lgradient
  end type line_function

contains

  real(REAL64) function lvalue(this,x)
    class(line_function) :: this
    real(REAL64), dimension(:), intent(in) :: x
    real(REAL64) :: a,b

    a = x(1)
    b = x(2)
    associate( x => this%x, y => this%y )
      lvalue = sum((y - a*x - b)**2)
    end associate

  end function lvalue

  subroutine lgradient(this,x,fgrad)
    class(line_function) :: this
    real(REAL64), dimension(:), intent(in) :: x
    real(REAL64), dimension(:), intent(out) :: fgrad
    real(REAL64) :: a,b

    a = x(1)
    b = x(2)
    associate( x => this%x, y => this%y )
      fgrad(1) = -sum( (y - a*x - b)*x )
      fgrad(2) = -sum( (y - a*x - b) )
    end associate

  end subroutine lgradient

end module lajna

program line

   use lajna
   use oakleaf

   real, dimension(5), target :: x = [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ]
   real, dimension(5), target :: y = [ 1.1, 2.2, 3.3, 4.2, 5.5 ]
   type(lajna), allocatable :: fcn
   real(REAL64), dimension(2) :: p
   real(REAL64), dimension(2,2) :: H
   real(REAL64) :: gtol
   integer :: iflag

   ! create the function
   fcn = line_function(x,y)
   ! only pointers on data are stored in the function

   ! initial estimate, p = [ a, b ]
   p = 0

   ! the tolerance for the norm of the gradient
   gtol = sqrt(epsilon(gtol))

   call bfgsmin(fcn,p,H,gtol,2*200,.true.,'',iflag)
   write(*,*) 'p=',p,'    iflag=',iflag
   write(*,*) 'H=',H
   write(*,*) 'residuals: ', y - (p(1)*x + p(2))

end program line
